options: The page is dirty in memory and nothing more
The data has reached the device
The data has reached the device's buffer
The data will reach the device within a bounded time
drills.why: Something eventually will send it, on a schedule nobody in the program chose, and the gap between those two facts is where a whole category of data loss lives.

drills.q: What does the page cache compete with for memory?
options: Every process's anonymous pages, under the same replacement policy
Nothing; it has a fixed reservation
Only other file mappings
The kernel's own allocations only
drills.why: Which is why a machine copying a large file evicts a program's data and then appears to have less memory than it did.

drills.q: Roughly how far apart are a page cache hit and a miss?
options: Three orders of magnitude
A factor of two
A factor of ten
Six orders of magnitude
drills.why: Tens of nanoseconds for a copy from memory against tens of microseconds for a device access, decided by whether somebody read it recently.

drills.q: What happens to the read-ahead window on a non-sequential access?
options: It collapses to one
It halves
It stays at its current size
It grows, on the assumption of a new sequence
drills.why: The evidence for the pattern is gone rather than weakened, and a program that jumps constantly disables the mechanism entirely and pays full latency per access.

drills.q: What happens when dirty pages cross the first threshold?
options: Background writeback starts and the program notices nothing
Writes begin to block
The kernel drops the oldest dirty pages
Reads slow down
drills.why: Only past the second threshold is a process made to write pages out itself, and that transition is abrupt.

drills.q: A program writes at memory speed for several seconds and then at device speed. What changed?
options: Nothing in the program; it filled the dirty page allowance
The device entered a thermal limit
The file grew past an extent boundary
The writeback thread was descheduled
drills.why: A benchmark short enough to stay under the threshold reports a number no sustained workload will ever see, which is the same shape as the write buffer in unit 039.

options: That file's dirty pages are written back and the device's buffer is flushed
That every dirty page in the system is written back
That the file and its directory entry are durable
That subsequent writes will also be durable
drills.why: It says nothing about the directory the file is in, so a newly created file can be fully written and flushed and still not exist after a power loss.

drills.q: What are the four steps of safely replacing a file?
options: Write the temporary, flush it, rename over the original, flush the directory
Write the temporary, rename, flush the directory
Write in place and flush
Delete the original, write the new one, flush
drills.why: Skip the directory flush and the rename is not durable. Skip the file flush and the name points at incomplete contents, which is worse than the file not existing.

drills.q: An fsync fails and you call it again. What happens?
options: It succeeds, because the error was reported once and cleared
It fails again
It blocks until the write succeeds
It returns a different error
drills.why: Not because anything was written. Several databases treated that second success as proof of durability and lost data for years.

drills.q: What is the current guidance on an fsync failure?
options: It is not retryable and the data must be assumed lost
Retry with exponential backoff
Reopen the file and retry
Fall back to a direct write
drills.why: Some systems treat it as fatal, which sounds extreme and is the only interpretation the interface supports.

drills.q: What orders two writes to different files?
options: Nothing, without a flush between them
The order the calls were made
The kernel's writeback queue
The device's completion order
drills.why: A program that writes a record and then a pointer to it can lose the record and keep the pointer, which is exactly the corruption a journal exists to prevent.

drills.q: Why is a system doing small durable updates limited by flushes rather than bandwidth?
options: Each flush costs the real device latency rather than the buffered one
Each flush writes the whole file
Flushes are serialised across the machine
Small writes have high amplification
drills.why: Batching several logical updates into one flush is the standard answer and it is why databases group commits.

drills.q: What must be aligned for a direct transfer?
options: The file offset, the length, and the memory buffer's address
The file offset only
The offset and the length
Nothing; alignment affects speed rather than correctness
drills.why: The device transfers whole blocks between the medium and the address you gave it, with nothing in between to fix a misalignment, so the call fails rather than being slow.

drills.q: Why do databases bypass the page cache?
options: They have their own buffer pool, and a second cache underneath duplicates it
The page cache is slower than direct access
The page cache does not support large files
To avoid the kernel's read-ahead
drills.why: The reason is duplication rather than overhead, and for anything that does not manage its own caching the page cache is better than what you would write.

Yes; mapped writes go straight to the device
Yes; the mapping is flushed on unmap
Only for shared mappings
drills.why: It removes the transition and the copy, and it introduces a failure mode the read path does not have: an I/O error becomes a signal rather than a return value.
